title: How to add a transition in Keynote on Mac: step by step for Keynote 15.4
metaTitle: How to Add a Transition in Keynote on Mac (Step by Step)
description: Learn how to add a transition in Keynote on Mac: pick a slide, choose an effect in the Animate sidebar, then change or remove it in Keynote 15.4.
targetKeyword: how to add a transition in keynote on mac
intro: To add a transition in Keynote on Mac, select the slide, click Add an Effect in the Animate sidebar, then scroll the list and choose a transition. Keynote plays a preview and puts a blue marker on that slide in the slide navigator.
tldr: Click the slide in the slide navigator, then click Add an Effect in the Animate sidebar.
Scroll the list and pick a transition. A preview plays, and a blue marker shows the slide has one.
To change a transition, click Change at the top of the Animate sidebar. To remove it, choose None.
The object-matching transition needs a duplicate slide. Press Command-D (⌘D), change the objects, then add the effect to the first slide.
Apple's Mac transition guide is written for Keynote 15.4, which requires macOS 26 or later.

blocks.text: Transitions are the motion that plays when one slide gives way to the next. In Keynote on Mac, you add them one slide at a time, or to a group of slides in one pass. The steps here follow Apple's Keynote User Guide for Mac, which is labeled for Keynote 15.4. If your window looks different, check your version first. Then read the labels closely, because the Animate sidebar is where almost every transition setting lives.
Check your Keynote and macOS versions first

Apple's transition guide for Mac is labeled for Keynote 15.4. Apple's What's new page says Keynote 15.4 for Mac requires macOS 26 or later, so an older Mac cannot run that version. To see your Keynote version, open the Keynote menu and look for About Keynote. Apple's sources do not confirm that label, so trust your own menu over this guide if they differ.

rows: Requires macOS 26 or later. Apple's Mac transition guide is written for this version.
Added fresh transitions and builds, including shift, radial wipe and character blur.
Uses an Animate button in the toolbar and a Transitions pop-up, starting from No Transition Effect.
blocks.caption: Version facts from Apple's What's new page and Keynote for iCloud guide

blocks.text: Apple's What's new page lists no transition changes for 15.4. The transition additions it documents came earlier, in Keynote 15.3. Those include shift, radial wipe and character blur. If your list shows those names, your Keynote is at least 15.3. If it does not, your labels may differ from this guide, and updating is the safer choice before a live talk.
Add a transition to one slide

Start in the slide navigator on the left. Click the thumbnail of the slide that needs the transition. Keynote applies the effect to whatever is selected, so check the selection before you open the sidebar. The slide on the canvas should be the one you meant to change.

Then open the Animate sidebar and click Add an Effect. Apple's guide uses those exact labels. If your window does not match, search the window for them. In the web version, Apple's iCloud guide puts an Animate button in the toolbar instead.

Scrolling the list is the slow part. Keynote plays a preview each time you choose an effect, so you can click through a few before you commit. Pick one style for the whole deck, or one style for each kind of break. Consistency reads as polish. Constant variety reads as noise, and your audience will remember the content, not the effect.

Once you choose a transition, the Animate sidebar shows its controls. Those controls depend on the transition itself. Apple gives duration and direction as examples, so one transition may offer both, one, or neither. Change a setting, then watch the preview before you change the next one. That order makes it clear which setting did what.
Choose a transition that suits your talk

Start with the talk, not the effect. A talk with clear section breaks suits one calm transition used at each break. A fast demo with many short slides usually needs less motion, so the transition should stay out of the way. Shift, radial wipe and character blur, the 15.3 additions, are worth a look if your deck is mostly text.

Test each candidate on a real slide, not a blank one. A blank slide hides the problems that matter, such as a photo that jumps or a title that sits too close to the edge. Keep your shortlist short. A few transitions give a deck a consistent feel. Too many make the audience notice the effects instead of the content.
Add the same transition to several slides

Select the slides in the slide navigator. Hold Shift or Command while you click, the same way you select files in Finder. Click Add an Effect in the Animate sidebar, then choose a transition. The effect goes to every slide you selected. Apple's Mac guide does not mention an Apply to All option, so do not hunt for one.

Think about the section openers first. Say your deck has a few section openers and the rest are content slides. Select only the openers, add one transition, and check their markers. Then scan the content slides and confirm they have none. This takes less time than adding a transition to each slide and removing it from the rest.
Set the timing and start option

Two settings matter most for timing. The first is duration, if your chosen transition offers it. Apple's guide gives duration as an example control, so check whether the effect has one. The second is Start Transition, which appears for some transitions. On Click waits for you. Automatically starts the move right after the previous slide advances, and a Delay field appears so you can set a pause.

Automatic start suits a display that runs without a presenter, such as a looping slideshow at a booth. Keep On Click for a live talk, so you control each move. Check the timing in a full-screen run. A pause that looks right in the sidebar can feel long once people are watching.
Change or remove a transition later

Changing a transition does not require removing it first. Select the slide, click Change at the top of the Animate sidebar, and choose a different transition. To remove the effect entirely, choose None. The blue marker should disappear once the slide has no transition left.

items: Select the slide in the slide navigator.
Click Change at the top of the Animate sidebar.
Choose a different transition, or choose None to remove it.
Check the slide navigator for the blue marker.

blocks.text: Set up an object-matching transition

Keynote also has an object-matching transition, which animates matching objects from one slide to the next. It needs two slides that share objects, such as shapes or text boxes. Apple's guide gives this effect a name that ends in Move, so scan the Add an Effect list for that entry. The setup starts with a duplicate, not with the sidebar.

items: Select the slide that holds the objects.
On one or both slides, change the objects. Move a shape, swap a word, or resize a text box.
Click Add an Effect in the Animate sidebar, then choose the entry whose name ends in Move.

blocks.text: The sidebar offers these controls for the object-matching effect. Learn them before you rehearse, because they change how the motion looks.

items: Duration: a slider for how long the move takes.
Fade Unmatched Objects: turn it off so objects with no match appear and disappear instantly.
Match: By Object, By Word, or By Character. Pick the level that fits your content.
Acceleration: None, Ease In, Ease Out, or Ease In & Ease Out.
Start Transition: On Click or Automatically. Automatically adds a Delay field.

blocks.text: Say your first slide has a phone image on the left and a headline across the top. Duplicate the slide with Command-D. On the copy, move the phone to the right and change the headline. Select the first slide, add the object-matching effect, and set Match to By Word. Words that exist on both slides should move into their new places. Run it at full screen before you trust it.
Keynote for iCloud uses different labels

Keynote for iCloud runs in a browser at iCloud.com. Apple's iCloud guide says you need a computer to use it, and tablets can only view files. The steps look different. Select the slide, click the Animate button in the toolbar, then click No Transition Effect in the Animate sidebar on the right. Pick an effect from the Transitions pop-up menu, then click Play to preview.

Apple's iCloud guide also suggests applying a transition to one blank slide, then duplicating it. The duplicates keep the transition, which saves time on a repeated layout. The iCloud pages list no keyboard shortcuts. Apple's Mac transition page lists only Command-D, so do not expect a full shortcut list in either version.
Why transitions look pixelated or stutter

A 2019 Apple Community thread describes pixelated Keynote transitions on a MacBook Pro running macOS 10.15.1. A reply gives the path Keynote > Preferences > Slideshow > Displaying, and says to uncheck Apply motion blur to animations. The original poster said that fixed it. Apple's current guide does not document this setting, and the thread never names a Keynote version.

The same thread has a top reply that blames leftover CleanMyMac files, and says Apple Support traced the problem there. The poster said the 10.15.2 update did not fix it, and the thread is closed. Read that as one person's account. Before you change any setting, confirm the menu names on your own Mac.
Test the transitions before you present

Play the slideshow from the first slide, and watch every transition at the speed you plan to present. A duration that looks fine in the sidebar can feel slow once a room is watching. Play through once without stopping, then fix only what looked wrong. Repeated fixes on the same slide add up, and it gets hard to track which setting changed.

If you present with presenter notes, rehearse in that mode too. You want to see the transition the way your audience sees it, while your notes stay on your own screen. The presenter notes guide covers that setup in more detail.
Common mistakes with Keynote transitions

items: Adding the effect to the wrong slide. Check which thumbnail is selected before you click Add an Effect.
Looking for an Apply to All button. Apple's Mac guide describes selecting slides, then adding one effect.
Expecting the object-matching transition to work without matching objects. It compares objects on the two slides, so unmatched content gives it little to animate.
Trusting the editor preview alone. Play the slideshow to see the effect at full screen.
Mixing up Keynote for iCloud and Keynote on Mac. The Animate button and Transitions pop-up belong to the browser version.

blocks.text: Next steps after you add transitions

With transitions set, the next job is usually the notes or the media. You can [add presenter notes](/how-to/add-presenter-notes-in-keynote) so the script sits on screen. If a slide needs a clip, read how to [add a video to a slide](/how-to/add-a-video-to-a-slide-in-keynote). When the deck goes out as a movie, the guide to [exporting a presentation as a movie](/how-to/export-a-presentation-as-a-movie-in-keynote) covers that step.

faq.question: Where is the transition option in Keynote on Mac?
faq.answer: Select a slide in the slide navigator, open the Animate sidebar, and click Add an Effect. Then scroll the list and choose a transition. If you cannot see the sidebar, look for an Animate control in the toolbar, which Apple's iCloud guide describes for the web version.

faq.question: Can I add a transition to every slide at once?
faq.answer: Yes. Select all the slides you want in the slide navigator, then click Add an Effect and choose a transition. Apple's Mac guide does not describe an Apply to All option, so you add the effect once per group of slides.

faq.question: How do I remove a transition in Keynote on Mac?
faq.answer: Select the slide, click Change at the top of the Animate sidebar, then choose None. The blue marker in the slide navigator should disappear once the slide has no transition.

faq.question: What is the difference between a transition and the object-matching transition?
faq.answer: A regular transition moves from one slide to the next as a whole. The object-matching transition animates matching objects between two slides, so you duplicate the first slide and change its objects. Apple's guide uses Command-D for the duplicate step, and the effect's name ends in Move.

faq.question: Does Keynote for iCloud work the same as Keynote on Mac?
faq.answer: No. In Keynote for iCloud you click the Animate button in the toolbar, then No Transition Effect, then pick an effect from the Transitions pop-up. Editing needs a computer, and tablets can only view files.

faq.question: Why do my Keynote transitions look pixelated?
faq.answer: A 2019 Apple Community thread on macOS 10.15.1 describes that problem and suggests unchecking Apply motion blur to animations. Apple's current guide does not document that setting, and the thread never named a Keynote version, so treat it as an unofficial fix.

faq.question: Which Keynote version added the newest transitions?
faq.answer: Apple's What's new page says Keynote 15.3 added fresh transitions and builds, including shift, radial wipe and character blur. Keynote 15.4 for Mac requires macOS 26 or later and lists no transition changes.

appliesTo: Keynote 15.4 for Mac on macOS 26 or later. Older versions and Keynote for iCloud use other labels.
requirements: A Mac with Keynote installed. Apple's Mac transition guide is labeled for Keynote 15.4.
macOS 26 or later for Keynote 15.4, as Apple's What's new page states.
A presentation open in Keynote on Mac, with the slide navigator visible.
For the object-matching transition: two slides that share objects, such as shapes or text boxes.

steps.name: Select the slide
steps.text: In the slide navigator on the left, click the thumbnail of the slide that needs the transition. Keynote applies the effect to whatever is selected when you add it, so check that only the right slide is selected.
steps.tip: Look at the canvas too. The slide shown there should be the one you meant to change.

steps.name: Open the Animate sidebar and click Add an Effect
steps.text: With the slide still selected, open the Animate sidebar. Click Add an Effect. Apple's Mac guide uses these labels, so look for them if your window looks different.
steps.tip: Apple's iCloud guide puts the Animate control in the toolbar, so check there if the sidebar is hidden.

steps.name: Scroll the list and choose a transition
steps.text: Scroll the list of transitions and click one. Keynote plays a preview on the slide, so you can judge the movement before you commit. Click another transition to compare.
steps.tip: Keep a short list of candidates. Click through them in order, then pick the one that fits the talk.

steps.name: Look for the blue marker
steps.text: Check the slide navigator. A blue marker appears in the corner of the slide thumbnail. That marker tells you the slide has a transition, so you can scan the deck for gaps.
steps.tip: If you see no marker, select the slide again and check the sidebar.

steps.name: Adjust the transition controls
steps.text: Use the controls that appear in the Animate sidebar. They depend on the transition you chose. Apple's examples are duration and direction, so expect a slider, a menu, or both. Change one setting at a time and watch the preview.
steps.tip: Pick a duration you would use while speaking. A move that looks fine in the sidebar can feel rushed on stage.

steps.name: Set Start Transition if the sidebar shows it
steps.text: If the sidebar offers Start Transition, choose On Click to advance by hand, or Automatically to start the move right after the previous slide advances. Automatically adds a Delay field.
steps.tip: Use On Click for a live talk. Automatic suits a display that runs by itself.

steps.name: Play the slideshow to check it
steps.text: Start the slideshow from the first slide with the Play control. Watch the transition at full screen, because the slideshow shows it the way your audience sees it. Play from the slide before the transition too, so you see the lead-in.
steps.tip: Note any transition that looks off, fix that one, then play again.

shortcuts.action: Duplicate a slide for object-matching setup

troubleshooting.problem: The transition is missing from the Add an Effect list
troubleshooting.fix: Check your Keynote and macOS versions. Apple's guide for Keynote 15.4 requires macOS 26 or later, and an older Mac may show different labels.

troubleshooting.problem: Only one slide got the transition
troubleshooting.fix: Select every slide that should have it before you click Add an Effect. Apple's Mac guide does not list an Apply to All option, so you add the effect once per group.

A 2019 Apple Community reply suggests unchecking Apply motion blur to animations under Keynote > Preferences > Slideshow > Displaying. Apple's current guide does not document this, so confirm the menu name on your Mac first. The thread is closed and the cause was never confirmed.

troubleshooting.problem: The object-matching transition does not animate the objects I expected
troubleshooting.fix: Check that both slides contain matching objects and that Match is set to the level you want: By Object, By Word, or By Character. Turn on Fade Unmatched Objects if you want the rest to fade instead of vanishing.

troubleshooting.problem: I cannot find the Animate sidebar
troubleshooting.fix: Make sure a slide is selected, then open the Animate control. Apple's iCloud guide shows the Animate button in the toolbar and the sidebar on the right, so look for the same layout on your Mac.
